fact_en: Using clean energy from the sun, wind, and water helps cut down the carbon dioxide that warms our Earth!
fact_bis: Ang paggamit og limpyo nga enerhiya gikan sa adlaw, hangin, ug tubig motabang pagkunhod sa carbon dioxide nga mopainit sa Kalibutan!

findings.note: title_bis "Hinaw nga Kusog" — hinaw in Cebuano is to WASH (one's hands), not clean-as-adjective (hinlo/limpyo). Body says "limpyo nga enerhiya" and sibling card ffct-29981 titles it "Hinlo nga Geothermal Energy", so the title word is wrong for "clean" in general.

fact_en: The hardness of a mineral simply means how hard it is to scratch!
fact_bis: Ang katig-a sa usa ka mineral mao kung unsa kalisod kini kalason o gasgason!

findings.note: title_bis "Katinig sa Mineral" — katinig is Tagalog for CONSONANT; Cebuano for hardness is katig-a. The card's own body uses "katig-a" correctly, and sibling cards ffct-29998/ffct-29999 title it "Tig-a"/"Katig-a", so the title is the outlier.

fact_en:
How do scientists measure how hard a mineral is?

They use the Mohs scale from 1 to 10 to measure mineral hardness!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagsukod sa mga siyentista sa katig-a sa mineral?

Gigamit nila ang Mohs scale gikan sa 1 hangtod 10 aron sukdon ang katig-a sa mineral!

findings.note: title_bis "Mohs Scale sa Katinig" — same Tagalog false friend: katinig = consonant, not hardness (katig-a). Body uses "katig-a" twice; title names a different thing.

fact_en:
How does a hardness test work with scratching?

A harder mineral can scratch a softer one, but a softer one cannot scratch a harder one!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagtrabaho ang pagsulay sa katig-a pinaagi sa paggasgas?

Makagasgas ang mas tig-a nga mineral sa mas humok, apan dili makagasgas ang mas humok sa mas tig-a!

findings.note: title_bis "Pagkalot nga Test sa Katinig" — katinig (Tagalog: consonant) again used for hardness; the body correctly says "katig-a", confirming the title word is the defect.

fact_en: A streak plate is a piece of unglazed porcelain tile used to make a mineral's streak!
fact_bis: Ang streak plate usa ka piraso sa wala-mabordahi nga porselana nga gigamit aron makuha ang streak sa mineral!

findings.note: Body: "wala-mabordahi nga porselana" = UN-EMBROIDERED porcelain (borda = embroidery). English is "unglazed porcelain tile", the one property that defines a streak plate. Nothing else in the card mentions glaze, so the defining property is unrecoverable from the Cebuano.

fact_en: Gold is a soft, heavy metal that never rusts! Because it stays shiny, it is super valuable for making jewelry.
fact_bis: Ang bulawan usa ka soft ug heavy nga metal nga dili magkalawang! Mao nga bililhon kaayo kini para sa mga alahas.

findings.note: title_bis "Bulawan nga Dili Makaunod" — unod is flesh/meat; "makaunod" names nothing like rust (taya / kalawang). The body's "dili magkalawang" is correct, so the title is the outlier.

fact_en: Some mountains are still rising a tiny bit each year because the tectonic plates are still moving!
fact_bis: Padayon pa nga nagtaas og gamay ang ubang bukid matag tuig kay nagalihok pa ang mga plate!

findings.note: title_bis "Bukid nga Mokatul pa" — katul/katol in Cebuano is to ITCH, so the title reads "mountains that still itch". English is "Mountains Still Rising"; the body's "nagtaas" is the correct word and shows the title is wrong.

fact_en:
How do mangroves stand in soft mud?

Many mangroves use tall, stilt-like roots to prop themselves up in the soft mud!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagtindog sa bakhaw sa humok nga lapok?

Daghang bakhaw mogamit og tag-as nga mga gamot nga morag tukod aron mosuporta sa ilang kaugalingon!

findings.note: title_bis "Mga Ugat nga Stilt" for "Mangrove Stilt Roots" — in Cebuano ugat is a VEIN/blood vessel (Tagalog false friend for root); the heading reads "stilt veins". The card's own body and emph_bis use the correct Cebuano gamot ("tag-as nga mga gamot nga morag tukod"), and the terms list carries the Tagalog form "ugat na nakatayo" beside gamot — so the title is the outlier. Corpus evidence: this same card set uses ugat for LEAF VEINS (ffct-04128 "Ugat sa Dahon"), and plant roots are gamot 462x vs ugat 39x, the ugat hits being almost all titles.

fact_en:
How do mangrove roots breathe in wet mud?

Since wet mud has little air, some roots poke upward to breathe in oxygen!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagginhawa sa mga gamot sa bakhaw sa basa nga lapok?

Tungod kay gamay ra ang hangin, ang ubang gamot mosulbong pataas aron makaginhawa og oxygen!

findings.note: title_bis "Ugat nga Moginhawa" for "Breathing Roots" — reads as "breathing veins" in Cebuano, naming a different organ than the card is about. Body uses gamot twice ("Unsaon pagginhawa sa mga gamot sa bakhaw...", "ang ubang gamot mosulbong pataas"), and the terms list pairs Tagalog "ugat na humihinga" with Cebuano "gamot nga ginhawa", so the Tagalog word leaked into the title only. Same systematic title defect as ffct-30163.

fact_en: The longer a grain is tumbled by waves, the finer, rounder, and smoother it becomes!
fact_bis: Kung mas dugay nga giligid sa balud ang usa ka lugas, mas pino, lingin, ug hamis kini!

findings.note: title_bis "Hamas nga Buto" for "Smooth Rounded Grains": `buto` is the Tagalog word for seed/bone; in Cebuano `buto` means an explosion/burst (and is vulgar slang), so the title names a different thing than the card is about. The card's own body uses the correct Cebuano word `lugas` ("Kung mas dugay nga giligid sa balud ang usa ka lugas, mas pino, lingin, ug hamis kini"), which is the evidence that the title is the outlier rather than regional variation. `Hamas` is also not a word (should be `hamis`, smooth), so the whole title fails to name the grain. Title-only defect; the body still delivers the fact.

fact_en:
Is fog really just a cloud on the ground?

Fog is a cloud that forms right at the ground, so walking through it feels like walking inside a cloud!
fact_bis:
Ang gabon ba panganod lang sa yuta?

Ang gabon usa ka panganod nga naporma sa yuta, mao nga morag naglakaw ka sulod sa panganod!

findings.note: title_en "Fog, a Ground Cloud" → title_bis "Yabo nga Panganod". In Cebuano yabo = to spill/pour out, not fog; the title reads "spilled cloud". The card's own body uses the correct word throughout ("Ang gabon usa ka panganod nga naporma sa yuta"), which is the evidence the title is the outlier. Corpus cross-check: yabo is used for SPILLING in Cebuano bodies elsewhere ("nayabo nga asido sa lab", "dili kini mayabo", "ang pag-yabo sa tubig gikan sa mga sudlanan"), and appears as "fog" ONLY in generated titles — the same broken title family also produced "Yabo Ulap Yuta" (ffct-28986) and "Dili Kayabo Adlaw" (ffct-28965, for "The Sun Isn't Fire", i.e. kalayo mangled). Systematic, ~8 cards corpus-wide.

fact_en:
What exactly is fog made of?

Fog is made of countless tiny water droplets floating in the air close to the ground!
fact_bis:
Unsa man gyud ang sulod sa gabon?

Ang gabon gilangkuban sa daghan kaayong gagmayng tinulo sa tubig nga naglutaw sa hangin duol sa yuta!

findings.note: title_en "What Fog Is Made of" → title_bis "Sulod sa Yabo" = "inside the spill". Same defect family as ffct-30354: yabo is spill, fog is gabon, and this card's own body says gabon correctly ("Ang gabon gilangkuban sa daghan kaayong gagmayng tinulo sa tubig"). The child cannot connect the heading to the card.
